section_summary: This section documents Japanese military administration and defensive restrictions in colonial Taiwan from 1933 to 1937, including changes of Taiwan Army commanders, fortified zones at Keelung and Takao, and extensive controls on photography and access to military areas. A large group of records concerns mounting fears of espionage: the arrest of Yo Ka To for attempting to sell a map, accusations against foreign residents and ships, press corrections obtained by the American consul, and the scrutiny of consular requests for ordinary information. The final records describe Taiwan’s placement on a wartime footing during the 1937 conflict in China, with blackouts, air defenses, censorship, internal surveillance, and reported air operations against China.

subfiles.title: Despatch reporting Iwane Matsui’s appointment as Taiwan Army commander
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival, career, and strategic views of Lieutenant General Iwane Matsui as the new commander-in-chief of the Taiwan Army.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham reports that Matsui arrived on August 21 to succeed Nobuyuki Abe, who had been transferred to the Supreme Military Council. The despatch outlines Matsui’s military career and quotes his warnings about Japan’s international position, China, and Taiwan’s role in southward expansion. It estimates Taiwan’s permanent garrison at 8,000–10,000 men and identifies its principal units and bases.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the attempted sale of a Keelung fortified-zone map
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes the arrest of a Formosan Chinese who approached the American Consulate offering a map of the Keelung fortified zone.
subfiles.summary: After receiving a suspicious letter, Ketcham had interpreter Matsuo notify the police and gendarmerie without personally interviewing the visitor. The man, who identified himself as Yo Ka To and said he came from the Canadian Presbyterian Mission School in Tamsui, was arrested in the consulate servants’ quarters. The Government-General, police, and gendarmerie approved the consul’s handling of the case.

subfiles.title: Letter from Yo Ka To to the American consul
subfiles.from: Yo Ka To
subfiles.about: A brief, poorly written approach to the American consul apparently connected with the proposed delivery or sale of a map.
subfiles.summary: Yo Ka To states that he has lived in Keelung for nearly nine months and has something ready to present if the consul agrees. The obscure wording reflects either limited English or faulty transcription and formed the documentary basis for the police referral.

subfiles.title: Department commendation of Ketcham’s action in the map case
subfiles.from: For the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John B. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Commends Ketcham for referring the attempted sale of a fortified-area map to the local police.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to Ketcham’s May 23 despatch concerning the Formosan Chinese who offered a map of a fortified area. It formally approves and commends his action.

subfiles.title: Despatch protesting press accounts of the Keelung map case
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports misleading newspaper allegations about the American Consulate’s role in the Yo Ka To case and the corrections secured from colonial officials.
subfiles.summary: After censorship of the case ended, three Taiwan newspapers published accounts implying that Ketcham had negotiated to buy the map and that police independently caught him doing so. Ketcham protested to Director General Hiratsuka, arguing that the stories suggested American espionage and damaged the consulate’s standing. Hiratsuka arranged instructions to the newspapers, which published corrections between September 8 and 12.

subfiles.title: Article: “Traitor Yo Ka Do Waived Right of Appeal”
subfiles.from: Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: Reports Yo Ka To’s five-year sentence and falsely credits police surveillance with discovering and stopping the map sale.
subfiles.summary: The article portrays Yo as an unemployed former English teacher radicalized in Shanghai and capable of drawing a detailed map from observation. It says he planned to sell the map to a consul for ¥2,000 and waived his right to appeal. It gives Yamada and the Kita Police Secret Service sole credit for detecting and arresting him.

subfiles.title: Two Taiwan Shimbun reports on the Yo Ka To case
subfiles.from: Taiwan Shimbun
subfiles.about: Presents allegations that Yo negotiated a map sale with the American Consulate and reports official warnings about similar crimes.
subfiles.summary: The first article claims that Yo repeatedly visited the consulate, contracted to sell the map for ¥2,000, and was arrested through a coordinated police operation; it also names a friend who allegedly inspired the scheme. A second item quotes Kita Police chief Inouye condemning Yo and promising strict vigilance during the expected international crisis. Both accounts obscure the consulate’s role in alerting the police.

subfiles.title: Article on the attempted sale of the Keelung fortified-zone map
subfiles.from: Tainan Shimpo
subfiles.about: Describes Yo Ka To’s conviction while implying that he was arrested during an attempted sale to Consul Ketcham.
subfiles.summary: The report places the case within broader rumors of espionage before Taiwan military maneuvers. It says Yo spent months investigating the fortified zone and was arrested after coming to Taihoku to offer the map for ¥2,000. The article incorrectly minimizes the consulate’s cooperation and contains biographical and chronological details inconsistent with the other accounts.

subfiles.title: Government-General memorandum recommending correction of press reports
subfiles.from: Secretary-Translator, Taiwan Government-General
subfiles.about: Records Ketcham’s protest and recommends publishing corrections affirming his lack of connection with Yo Ka To and his cooperation with police.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts Ketcham’s meeting with Hiratsuka and his objection that the September 5 articles implicated him in espionage. Ketcham asked that newspapers state both that he had no connection with the culprit and that he had voluntarily helped secure the arrest. The drafter finds the request reasonable and submits a proposed correction for approval.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to three Taiwan newspapers
subfiles.from: Chief, Division of Records and Archives, Taiwan Government-General
subfiles.to: Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo Sha; Taiwan Shimbun Sha; Tainan Shimpo Sha
subfiles.about: Orders the newspapers to correct their accounts of the American consul’s conduct in the Yo Ka To case.
subfiles.summary: The draft states that the September 5 stories could create public suspicion about the American consul. It directs each paper to clarify that the consul had no connection with Yo or his acts and cooperated with the police from the beginning.

subfiles.title: Correction acknowledging American Consulate cooperation
subfiles.from: Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: Corrects the suggestion that the American Consulate had arranged to purchase Yo Ka To’s map.
subfiles.summary: The article repeats Yo’s conviction but states that the American Consulate cooperated in his arrest. It records Ketcham’s insistence that neither he nor the consulate had any connection with the culprit and notes that the original lead apparently came from the consulate.

subfiles.title: Taiwan Shimbun corrections concerning Yo Ka To
subfiles.from: Taiwan Shimbun
subfiles.about: Publishes corrections clearing the American consul of involvement in the attempted map sale.
subfiles.summary: The paper corrects its September 5 article by declaring that the consul had no connection with Yo or his crime. It adds that the consul cooperated with the police from the beginning and that government authorities respected his conduct.

subfiles.title: Tainan Shimpo correction clearing the American consul
subfiles.from: Tainan Shimpo
subfiles.about: States that investigation established the American consul’s innocence and cooperation with the police.
subfiles.summary: The correction notes the sensation caused by the case amid international spy fears. It concludes that the consul had no connection with Yo’s action and instead assisted the police from the outset.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on the Juno enclosure
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs staff member
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the report that lawyers who defended the Juno in an espionage case would no longer be permitted to practice in military courts.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten note particularly highlights the final enclosure associated with the Taiwan spy-scare despatch. Its focus is the professional punishment imposed on the attorneys who defended the Danish tanker Juno.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding reports on espionage warnings in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Forwards a military officer’s anti-espionage speech and a report illustrating the severity with which spy cases were treated.
subfiles.summary: Maney sends translations of a speech by a Taiwan Military Headquarters staff officer and of a second newspaper article. He adds that virtually every consular request for information was being submitted to military headquarters for approval, regardless of subject or recipient.

subfiles.title: Speech: “The Days of Activities of Spies”
subfiles.from: Major Hattori, as reported by Taiwan Shimbun
subfiles.to: Taihoku Federal Reservist Association and public readership
subfiles.about: Warns that foreigners, officials, ships, missionaries, and ordinary requests for information may all serve espionage purposes.
subfiles.summary: Hattori argues that spies cannot be identified by nationality, sex, occupation, outward behavior, or the absence of physical evidence. He treats foreign diplomatic requests, port visits, photography, surveying, and even defenses of accused foreigners as possible threats to national security. The speech calls for systematic study of foreign espionage networks and national unity in suppressing suspected spying.

subfiles.title: Report on punishment of lawyers in the Juno case
subfiles.from: Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo and Taiwan Shimbun
subfiles.about: Reports the removal of two Juno defense lawyers from military-court practice and the questioning of a doctor who criticized the case.
subfiles.summary: The War Department removed lawyers Chūki Ampo and Keitoku Nagao from the approved military-court bar because they defended the Juno case. Army officers also summoned Dr. Miyabara after he allegedly called the case insignificant from the standpoint of a great nation, and he apologized.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to warning about the Pescadores and Mako Naval Port
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file concerning an official warning against entering or anchoring near the Pescadores Islands and Mako Naval Port.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a February 5, 1936 communication from Maney. The referenced document concerns restrictions on entry and anchorage around the strategically important Pescadores and Mako naval base.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Department note on suspicion arising from Maney’s inquiries
subfiles.from: Unidentified Department of State official
subfiles.about: Comments that Maney’s requests for road and motor-car information had predictably generated military suspicion.
subfiles.summary: The writer had held the matter while expecting a related despatch and was not surprised that Maney’s statistical inquiries caused suspicion. The note also says that instructions sent to Tokyo several weeks earlier should by then have been acted upon.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the increasing virulence of Taiwan’s “spy mania”
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes several incidents illustrating intensified suspicion of foreigners and contacts with the American Consulate.
subfiles.summary: Maney reports rumors against Professor Arundell del Re, military surveillance that forced statistician T. Hariguchi to end contact with the consulate, and criticism of Mrs. Ishimoto for visiting Mrs. Maney. He also recounts the detention of the Norwegian ship Unita after entering Su’ao and an implausible report that spies were planting underground explosives in Taipei. Maney concludes that these episodes reveal a widening climate of anti-espionage suspicion.

subfiles.title: Article accusing Professor del Re of suspicious translation work
subfiles.from: Toa Shimpo
subfiles.about: Repeats rumors that Professor Arundell del Re used female students to translate Japanese publications for possible espionage purposes.
subfiles.summary: The article compares the rumor with earlier Taiwan spy scares and allegations involving a foreign military attaché. It suggests that del Re could clear himself only by publicly disclosing the translations and insinuates that his academic and commercial activities might conceal espionage. The writer nevertheless expresses a hope that the rumor will prove false.

subfiles.title: Despatch on military regulations governing photography in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Forwards and confirms a Taiwan Army regulation restricting aerial and elevated photography in designated areas.
subfiles.summary: Maney encloses a translation of the regulation and a map marking the affected areas. Although the text had been obtained from a newspaper, the consulate secured verbal confirmation of its authenticity from military authorities.

subfiles.title: Regulation prohibiting aerial photography in designated areas
subfiles.doc_type: Translated military regulation and newspaper clipping
subfiles.from: Taiwan Army, reported by Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: Prohibits aerial and high-place photography and distribution of images covering extensive parts of Taiwan and its offshore islands.
subfiles.summary: The regulation requires prior gendarmerie direction and inspection of aerial photographs before sale or distribution, with surrender of prohibited negatives. It defines eleven extensive prohibited areas covering northern, eastern, central, and southern Taiwan, the Pescadores, offshore islands, and adjacent territorial waters. Violators were to be treated as traitors by cooperating gendarmes and police.

subfiles.title: Consular map of Taiwan photography-prohibition areas
subfiles.from: Tan Ko Heng, American Consulate, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Maps Taiwan’s cities, mountains, islands, and other features in connection with military photography restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The consular map provides island-wide geographical context for the areas affected by the Taiwan Army’s regulation. It marks major settlements, mountain peaks, the Pescadores, and Taiwan’s surrounding waters.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding a magazine article insinuating foreign espionage
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards an article whose presentation encouraged readers to infer that numerous foreign visitors to Taiwan were spies.
subfiles.summary: Maney describes the article as subtly worded but notes that its prominent “Spies?” caption likely implicated all the foreigners mentioned. He sends a translation to the embassy and copies it to the Department and Consulate General.

subfiles.title: Magazine article cataloguing suspicious foreign visitors
subfiles.from: Taiwan Jitsugyo Kai (Taiwan Business World)
subfiles.about: Lists foreign travelers, consular officers, merchants, naval wives, and photographers treated as potential spies in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The article says foreigners could reasonably be regarded as spies and recounts suspicious travel or inquiries by British, American, Russian, and other visitors. It describes restrictions on foreigners landing at Keelung, close scrutiny of photography from scheduled aircraft, and warnings about confidential railway maps. Even social contact with an English-speaking dancer is presented as grounds for surveillance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to invasion of the Taihoku consulate by a blackout guard
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe, Taihoku
subfiles.about: References a despatch concerning a light-control guard’s unauthorized entry into the American Consulate.
subfiles.summary: The sheet notes that a Taihoku blackout or light-control guard entered the consulate on the night of June 28. Authorities were approached and steps were reportedly taken to prevent recurrence; copies of news reports accompanied the original despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch on designation of the Takao fortified zone
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the creation, boundaries, and practical significance of a large fortified zone around Takao.
subfiles.summary: Rowe reports that joint War and Navy Notice No. 6 established a fortified zone encompassing roughly sixty miles of coast, extending up to thirty miles inland, and including Ryukyusho. He identifies the boundary localities and the principal cities within the zone. Because photography and sketching restrictions were rigidly enforced and had caused problems for foreigners, he recommends publicizing the zone.

subfiles.title: Notice No. 6 establishing the Takao military-defense zone
subfiles.from: Hajime Sugiyama, Minister of War; Mitsumasa Yonai, Minister of the Navy
subfiles.about: Legally establishes the boundary around military defense structures at Takao under the Fortification Zone Law.
subfiles.summary: The notice fixes the protected boundary at 3,500 ken inside the dotted line shown on the official map. It orders that the limits be physically marked with signposts and cites the relevant provisions of the Fortification Zone Law.

subfiles.title: Official Gazette map of the Takao fortified zone
subfiles.from: Government-General of Taiwan Official Gazette
subfiles.about: Shows the legally defined Takao fortified zone and nearby places on the published official-gazette map.
subfiles.summary: The reproduced gazette map marks the fortified area around Takao with reference to the Nisokokei River, Okayama, Suikaen, Choshu, Ryukyusho, and Senninzuka. It accompanies the translated War and Navy notice and supplies the authoritative boundary diagram.

subfiles.title: Consular map locating the Takao fortified zone within Taiwan
subfiles.from: Tan Ko Heng, American Consulate, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Provides an island-wide map showing the Takao fortified zone in relation to the rest of Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The map combines major cities, rivers, islands, and mountain peaks with an inset-like depiction of the southern fortified area. It was prepared at the American Consulate to clarify the zone’s location and geographical scale.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Taiwan’s wartime mobilization during the China conflict
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the new Taiwan Army commander’s arrival and the colony’s placement on a wartime footing amid the conflict in China.
subfiles.summary: Rowe describes Motoo Furushō’s career, his replacement of Shunroku Hata, and his inflammatory public comparison of military action in China to a necessary operation. Furushō’s proclamation announces wartime duties, demands loyalty and anti-espionage vigilance, and threatens those spreading rumors or making allegedly unpatriotic statements. The despatch details air-defense preparations, blackouts, armed guards, coastal restrictions, censorship of coded telegrams, surveillance of Chinese residents, and multilingual radio propaganda aimed at South China.

subfiles.title: Despatch on continuing Taiwan air operations and the China conflict
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports nightly departures of Taiwan-based aircraft toward China and rumors that replacement planes concealed combat losses.
subfiles.summary: The fragment says conditions in Taiwan had changed little since the August 17 report. Squadrons of about six aircraft were observed leaving the Taihoku army air base toward the northwest, reportedly for operations connected with attacks such as the bombing of Nanking. A rumor held that losses in China were concealed by sending replacement aircraft from Heito to join returning formations before they reached Taiwan; the document continues beyond the surviving page.
